opus-5.5.text:
I think what's fascinating is that it wasn't really planned that way. Lean started at Microsoft Research with Leo de Moura, and the original motivation was very much in the software verification world: proving that programs do what they're supposed to do. Leo had built Z3, the SMT solver, so he came from that tradition of automated reasoning for software.

What happened is that mathematicians discovered it, and the community took on a life of its own. Kevin Buzzard at Imperial was a big catalyst. He started getting undergraduates to formalize math and evangelizing it to working mathematicians. Then you had Mathlib, this enormous, community-built library of formalized mathematics that just kept growing. Once a library like that reaches critical mass, it becomes self-reinforcing. People formalize new results because the foundations they need are already there.

Then there were some really visible moments, like the Liquid Tensor Experiment, where Peter Scholze challenged the community to formalize a hard result he wasn't fully sure about, and they did it. That showed it wasn't just a toy for undergrad exercises; it could handle research-level math.

The part I find most interesting from our perspective is that the two worlds are converging again. Mathematics turned out to be an incredible proving ground for this technology. It's a domain where you have extremely hard reasoning, rich structure, and an absolute ground truth: the proof checks or it doesn't. That makes it a perfect environment for training AI systems to reason. And the same machinery that verifies a theorem about number theory can verify that a piece of software is correct. So in a sense Lean's detour through mathematics may end up being what makes verified software practical at scale. The math community built the infrastructure and the culture, and now AI can bring that back to the problem Lean was originally designed for.

r002.rationale: It describes the goal as proving that programs do what they are supposed to do, which communicates that verification proves software properties.

r003.rationale: It calls Mathlib a community-built library of formalized mathematics, but does not characterize it as an open-source mathematics textbook.

r004.rationale: It says mathematics may help make verified software practical, but does not suggest Lean is now used more for mathematics than for software verification.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the thing that's really striking about Lean is that it was never designed to become the lingua franca of mathematics. Leo de Moura built it at Microsoft Research as a programming language and a proof assistant, and the original motivation was much closer to software verification, to proving properties about programs, than to formalizing the Langlands program or whatever.

And what happened, I think, is a bit of an accident of community. Kevin Buzzard at Imperial started playing with it around 2017, and he had this very specific frustration, which was that he felt like mathematicians couldn't actually verify the proofs they were citing. He'd say, look, there are results in my field that rest on papers nobody has fully checked, and we just trust them because the author is well regarded. Lean gave him a way to take that complaint seriously. And he was loud about it, in a good way, and he pulled in undergrads, and the undergrads built Mathlib.

Mathlib is really the key piece. The tool itself is nice, the dependent type theory is expressive, the tactic framework is good, but the reason mathematicians use Lean rather than Coq or Isabelle is that someone already formalized the definition of a topological space, a scheme, a perfectoid space, the whole stack, in one coherent library with one set of conventions. That's a social achievement as much as a technical one. Thousands of contributors, a very opinionated review process, and a norm that you build on the shared library rather than forking off.

Then the thing that pushed it over the edge was Peter Scholze's Liquid Tensor Experiment. He basically said, here's a proof I'm not sure about, it's at the foundation of a lot of my work, can you check it. And the community did it in about a year and a half. That was the moment where it stopped being a hobby for a handful of people and became something serious mathematicians took seriously.

And from where I sit, the interesting second-order effect is that you now have this enormous corpus of machine-checkable mathematics, which turns out to be exactly what you want if you're trying to train models to do math. The verifier gives you a reward signal that doesn't lie. So a tool built to check software ends up being the substrate for AI doing mathematics, which nobody planned, and that's kind of the beautiful part of it.

r003.rationale: It describes Mathlib as a community-built shared library of formalized mathematics, but does not characterize it as an open-source mathematics textbook.

r004.rationale: It describes Lean’s growing role in mathematics and AI, but does not suggest that its mathematical use may exceed its use for software verification.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that software verification and mathematics turn out to need a lot of the same machinery. In both cases, you’re trying to state something precisely and give an argument that a computer can check. But the way people use that machinery can be quite different.

For software, you might want to prove that a program satisfies a specification. In mathematics, the proof itself is often the thing you care about. So the challenge becomes: can you express the concepts naturally, build on existing results, and work at a level where you’re thinking about the mathematics rather than every tiny logical step?

That makes the community and the library really important. Each formalized result gives the next person something to build on. As that grows, formalizing new mathematics becomes more practical, which attracts more people, who contribute more results. I think that’s the compelling part of the transition: a tool for checking correctness becomes a shared language for building mathematics.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that software verification and mathematics share this underlying problem: how do you know that a complicated argument is actually correct? Lean gives you a way to make every step precise enough that a computer can check it.

But the needs of those communities are different. A mathematician wants to express abstract ideas naturally, build on existing results, and avoid getting buried in bookkeeping. So the shift is as much about the library and the community around Lean as it is about the proof checker itself.

And that creates an interesting feedback loop. As more mathematics gets formalized, it becomes easier to formalize the next result. You’re building a foundation that other people—and potentially AI systems—can use, with a very clear standard for whether an argument works.
